Day streak 4

Blob cards

Your job: look at two brain blobs and say which one is rarer. Rarer means the blob is in the top 5 percent on more of the 39 tests (brain maps from the other games).

Every one of the 434 parts of the brain map is a blob, and every blob has a trading card. Some blobs are legendary and only 18 of those exist. Open a pack of five cards. Two blobs face each other and you say which is rarer. Then one blob faces two game pages and you say where it starred.

You play against the collector. It picks the bigger blob, and the page with more tests on it (a coin toss on a tie). Big does not mean rare, so over a pack the collector is right about 64 times in 100, and guessing gets 50. Your clue is the map: it is painted by team, and some teams hold far more rare blobs than others. A computer reading only the team is right 75 times in 100 on the blob rounds, so place is a strong nudge and not a promise. Your first card comes with a short tour. Three free hints wait on every card. At the end the rarer blob of each blob round and the blob of each page round go on your shelf.

    This part is written the way the lab writes. Skip it if you like.

    Words you will meet here
    blob, region, parcel
    one named patch of the brain map. There are 434 of them.
    test
    one of 39 brain maps taken from the other games (also called a quantity). Every blob gets a score on each one.
    percentile
    where a blob ranks among all 434. The 95th percentile means it beats 95 of every 100 blobs.
    top 5 %
    the best 1 in 20 blobs on a test. A blob that is in the top 5 % on 4 or 5 tests is in the rare tier here (6 or more is epic or legendary).
    tier
    the card class (common to legendary), set by how many tests a blob is in the top 5 % on.
    superpowers
    a blob's five best percentiles (the five tests where it ranks highest).
    rarity
    how many of the 39 tests put a blob in the best 1 in 20 (5 %). More tests means a rarer card.
    toy
    a simple summary made for play, not the lab's careful method.
    rest hubness
    how strongly a blob is linked to all the other blobs while a person rests in the scanner.
    night-to-night reliability
    how much a blob's links to the other blobs look the same from one night to the next.
    verb generation
    a task where you say a verb that goes with a noun you are shown. It is one of the 39 tests.
    noun reading
    a task where you read nouns aloud. It is one of the 39 tests.
    paper words
    the words that papers about a blob use most. Neurosynth counts them.
    Neurosynth fame
    how many Neurosynth papers mention a blob's words, shown as the share of papers with a peak there. It is a paint option in this notebook.
    Glass-pattern search
    a task where people look for a swirly pattern of dots. It is one of the 39 tests.
    fusiform
    the fusiform gyrus, a fold on the underside of the temporal lobe, behind the ear.
    cerebellum
    the small brain at the back, under the big one
    whole-region average
    one number for a whole blob, averaged over all of its tiny cubes
    MSC
    a study where ten people were scanned many nights. MSC01 is person number 1.
    network, team
    a team of regions that tend to rise and fall together. The map has eight teams; the eighth, the cerebellum, is not a network of the brain's outer layer but gets a row of its own.
    Neurosynth
    a robot librarian that counts which words appear in papers that found a peak in a blob.
    log-odds
    how much more often a word shows up near this blob than elsewhere. Bigger means a stronger link.
    Fisher z
    a link score between two regions at rest, stretched so it is easy to average.
    centroid
    the middle point of a blob, given as three numbers (left-right, back-front, down-up).
    MNI
    the standard brain grid that puts every scan in the same place, so the three centroid numbers mean the same spot for everyone.
    z
    a score in steps from the average blob: 0 is average and each step up is a bigger lead. Some tests print it with the word z.
    voxel
    one tiny cube of a brain scan (2 mm on a side).
    fROI read
    reading a person's own most responsive spots, the lab's stricter method.
    Crus
    Crus I and Crus II are two big folds of the cerebellum.
    schizophrenia, bipolar, ADHD
    three brain conditions that some of the scanned groups in other games have; the notebook paint menu lets you color blobs by how those groups differ from the other people.
    LH_, RH_ names
    atlas codes (short names from the atlas) for regions; LH is left and RH is right.
    team ladder
    the eight teams sorted by the average rarity of their blobs (tests in the top 5 %, averaged over the team's blobs).
    team rule, place clue
    pick the blob whose team sits higher on the ladder, with the two blobs of the round left out of the averages. It is a clue and not the answer.
    size rule
    pick the bigger blob. It is what the collector does on blob rounds.
    words rule
    pick the page that shares a topic word with the blob's three paper words. It is a clue and not the answer.
    practice rounds, seeded
    made-up rounds dealt the way the game deals them, to measure how often a rule is right. Seeded means the dealing starts from a fixed number, so the same practice rounds come out every time.
    build script
    the short program that made this page and measured the rules.
    peak
    the spot where a paper says the brain was most active.
    paint by, paint option
    a menu in this notebook that colors every blob by one measure, such as rarity.
    atlas
    the map that cuts the brain into the 434 blobs and gives each a name.
    base rate, chance
    how often a guess is right with no clues at all; with two choices it is 1 in 2, or 50 in 100.
    collector
    the player you play against. It picks the bigger blob or the page with more tests, and tosses a coin on a tie.

    Read this first

    The round. A blob round shows two blobs from two different tiers, lettered and outlined on the map, and asks which is rarer. Rarer means more of the 39 tests put the blob in the best 1 in 20 of all 434 blobs. The blobs' cards (size, team, words, tier) stay face down until you answer. A page round shows one blob and two pages and asks where it starred.

    The clues, measured. The map is painted by team because place is the clue: some teams hold far more rare blobs than others (Visual leads the ladder). Picking the blob whose team has the higher average rarity, with the two blobs on screen left out of the averages, is right 75 times in 100 over 2000 practice rounds drawn the way the game draws them (guessing gets 50). Size is not a clue: the bigger blob is the rarer one only 56 times in 100, and that is the collector's whole method. On page rounds the blob's three paper words mark the pages that share a topic word; picking the marked page (a coin when none or both are marked, which happens in 42 in 100 rounds for none) is right 65 times in 100 over 5840 practice rounds (292 blobs, 20 draws each). The team's favorite page is right 82 times in 100, and the collector's busier page 75. Both clues are right at least 60 times in 100, the bar we set for showing a clue, so both are offered on the round screen.

    History. The game started with four blobs from four tiers and four pages per round. The collector was right 28 times in 100 over a pack and the words rule 45 (guessing got 25), and players mostly guessed. In this version every round became a choice of two, the cards went face down, the map got painted by team, and the rules above were measured on seeded practice rounds that the page can repeat (seeded: dealt from a fixed starting number).

    How rare is rare?

    Rarity counts how many of the 39 tests put the blob in the top 5 % of all 434 blobs. "Superpowers" are its five best percentiles. The percentiles also compare regions of wildly different sizes.

    Toy warning: every number here is a whole-region average. The lab's real analyses use a stricter method called an fROI read.

    How this was made (lab skills used)

    This panel is for the lab. It names the tools and steps we used, in the lab's own words.

    Data. Nothing new was scanned or fitted for this page. Every number is lifted from the other pages of this collection and ranked across regions. The sources are Midnight Scan Club ds000224 for task z and the rest connectome, studyforrest ds000113 for the film annotations and ISC, Partly Cloudy ds000228 for theory of mind > pain per age, Wakeman & Henson ds000117 for faces, Narratives Pie Man ds002345 for story ISC, AOMIC PIOP1 ds002785 for the sex and age signal, UCLA CNP ds000030 for diagnosis d and Kamitani ds001246 for object decoding. The words come from the Neurosynth v7 release (Yarkoni et al. 2011). That release has 14,371 studies and 507,891 reported peaks and abstract tf-idf term features.

    Pipeline. The code is in pipelines/blobcards/. 01_collect.py reads each page's region-level asset file (assets/<mode>/). It aligns 39 tests to the shared 434-region atlas (Schaefer-400 cortex + 34 SUIT cerebellar regions) and converts each to a percentile across the regions that have a value. Ties are averaged. The five strongest rest partners per region come from the MSC group-mean connectome. 02_neurosynth.py maps every Neurosynth peak (stored in MNI) to a voxel of the 2 mm MNI152NLin6Asym atlas grid. A study hits a region when it reports at least one peak inside it. 72.2 % of peaks fall inside a region and the rest are subcortical or white matter or outside the atlas. A term is "on" for a study when its abstract tf-idf exceeds 0.001. The association for each region and term is the smoothed log-odds of "term on" among studies hitting the region versus the others. It needs at least 5 studies and is ranked per region. The brief asked for the 200 most frequent cognitive terms after a short stoplist. The vocabulary's most frequent entries turned out to be generic English and method words. So a curated candidate list of cognitive and perceptual and motor and clinical terms was intersected with the vocabulary and its 200 most frequent members were kept. Anatomy and method words were never candidates. 03_build_page.py writes assets/blobcards/cards.json and this page.

    Lab skills used. None were used directly. This page is built from the other modes' assets. The skills that produced those numbers (firstlevel, secondlevel, outlier, sandbox) are named on the pages they belong to. The shared viewer (common/) draws the fsaverage5 brain meshes and the SUIT flatmap. Nothing is measured on them.

    Caveats. Every test is a whole-atlas-region mean or a per-parcel statistic. It is a toy summary and not a subject-specific functional ROI. Parcels differ a lot in size so the percentiles compare unequal things. Some pages are small. Faces has 8 people and object decoding has 5 and the MSC tasks have 10. Some tests are weak maps whose top region is barely above noise. Screen brightness and ADHD vs controls and age in 18-26-year-olds are the weak ones. A "top 1 %" pill there means first among near-equals and not a strong effect. Neurosynth counts are whole-region hit counts from automatically extracted coordinates and abstract words. They inherit the atlas so the lower cerebellum and the nuclei are almost never hit. They say which words co-occur with peaks here and not what the region does. The rarity tiers are a game mechanic and nothing more.

    These are real brains from OpenNeuro. The numbers come from the 3-D scans and the pretty pictures are only pictures. Hover or tap a region for its name.
